blocks.prompt: The Loop That Makes the Light Come On
blocks.text: A bulb will not light on its own. It needs a loop. The loop starts at the battery, runs along a wire, goes through the bulb, and comes back to the battery. That loop is called a circuit. Inside the bulb is a tiny curl of wire called a filament. It is thinner than a hair. When electricity pushes through the filament, it gets very hot. It gets so hot that it glows white. That glow is your light. A switch is a small gap in the loop. Open the gap and the light goes out. Close the gap and the loop is whole again. The bulb comes back on right away.

a filament

blocks.prompt: Why the Light Comes On
blocks.text: Everything around you is made of atoms, and atoms carry tiny pieces called electrons. In a metal wire, some of those electrons are loose. They can move from atom to atom. That moving is what we call electric current. Current will not go anywhere unless it has a way out and a way back. That is why a circuit has to be a loop. A battery pushes the loose electrons out of one end, along the wire, through whatever you have put in the way, and back into the other end. Not every material lets electrons move. Copper does, which is why wires are made of copper. Rubber does not, which is why the wire has a rubber coat that is safe to hold. Materials that let current through are called conductors. Materials that block it are called insulators. A good circuit needs both, one to carry the current and one to keep it where it belongs. Inside an old style bulb, the wire suddenly gets very thin. The electrons have to squeeze through, and squeezing makes heat. The thin wire is made of a metal called tungsten. It glows white at around 2,500 degrees Celsius and still does not melt. That is the whole trick. The light is a wire being made to struggle.

answers: electric current
current needs a way out and a way back, so the path has to return to the battery
a conductor lets current through and an insulator blocks it
(inference: a thin wire makes the electrons squeeze, which makes heat and light)

blocks.prompt: The Frog Leg That Led to the Battery
blocks.text: In the 1780s an Italian doctor named Luigi Galvani was working on a dead frog. When he touched its leg with a metal instrument, the leg kicked. Galvani was astonished. He decided that animals must store a special force inside them, and he called it animal electricity. Another Italian, Alessandro Volta, read Galvani's work and did not believe a word of it. Volta noticed something Galvani had walked straight past. The kick only happened when two different metals touched the frog at the same time. Volta thought the electricity was coming from the metals, not from the animal. The frog was simply a wet path between them. To prove it, Volta got rid of the frog. In 1800 he stacked a disc of zinc, then a disc of copper, then a piece of cardboard soaked in salt water, and he repeated that pattern over and over into a tall column. When he touched a wire to the top and to the bottom, current flowed, and it kept on flowing. He had built the first battery. We call it the voltaic pile. This mattered far more than it sounds. Before Volta, the only electricity anyone could produce came in sudden sparks that were over in an instant. You could be startled by it, but you could not use it. Volta gave the world a steady push that could be sent along a wire and put to work, and every circuit you have ever switched on begins with a source like his. We even measure that push in volts. Galvani was not completely wrong, by the way. Nerves really do carry electrical signals, and your own muscles move because of them. He simply had the wrong explanation for his frog.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Electrons drift slower than a walking ant

Series: one loop, shared by all
Parallel: every branch gets its own loop

blocks.prompt: The Slowest Fast Thing in Your House
blocks.text: Flick a switch and the light appears instantly. It is tempting to picture electrons racing along the wire like water down a hose. They do not. In a copper wire carrying an ordinary household current, the electrons drift forward at less than a millimeter per second. An ant could outrun them. A single electron leaving your light switch might take hours to arrive at the bulb. So why is the light instant? Because the wire is already packed with loose electrons from end to end, like a tube already full of marbles. Push one marble in at your end and a marble drops out the far end immediately, even though no single marble crossed the tube. The push travels close to the speed of light. The electrons themselves barely shuffle. That push meets resistance. Every material fights the current a little, and a thin wire fights harder than a thick one. Fighting produces heat. In a toaster or an old bulb that heat is the entire point. Everywhere else it is waste. Now think about how you wire two bulbs. Put them both in a single loop, one after the other, and you have a series circuit. Take one bulb out and the loop is broken, so both go dark. Old strings of holiday lights were wired this way, which is why one dead bulb could kill the whole string. Give each bulb its own loop back to the source instead and you have a parallel circuit. Remove one and the other keeps glowing. Your house is wired in parallel. That is why a blown lamp in the hallway does not darken the kitchen. Parallel wiring carries a danger. Every loop you add pulls more current through the main wire, and more current means more heat. Worse is a short circuit, where a stray path lets current skip past the bulb and run straight home with almost nothing to slow it down. The current climbs, the wire heats, and a house fire is one melted insulator away. So we build a deliberate weak point into the loop. A fuse is a thin strip of metal chosen to melt and break the circuit before the rest of the wiring gets dangerous. A circuit breaker does the same job with a switch that trips. Both exist to fail, so that nothing else has to.

6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Loop That Makes the Light Come On

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Circuit: from Latin for a going around
Volta's pile, 1800: the first steady current
Ohm's law, 1827: push, current, resistance
Transistor, 1947, Bell Labs
Integrated circuit: Kilby 1958, Noyce 1959
A phone chip holds tens of billions of switches

blocks.prompt: From a Stack of Coins to Ten Billion Switches
blocks.text: The word circuit comes from a Latin word meaning a going around, and after two centuries of invention that definition has never once needed changing. A circuit is a loop. Current leaves a source, passes through something that puts it to use, and returns. Break the loop anywhere and everything stops. That single rule governs a flashlight and it governs the processor in your phone, and nothing in between has escaped it. The loop needed a source, and in 1800 it got one. Alessandro Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by cardboard soaked in brine, and found that his column pushed a steady current through a wire for as long as he cared to leave it connected. Before the voltaic pile, electricity meant static sparks: dramatic, useless, and finished in an instant. Volta's stack gave a push that lasted, which meant electricity could finally be studied rather than merely admired. Studying it produced a law. In 1827 Georg Ohm published the relationship that still describes every loop ever built: the current depends on the push driving it and the resistance opposing it. Double the push and you double the current. Double the resistance and you halve it. German scientists dismissed his work as a fantasy at the time. The unit of resistance is now named after him. Then the loop got a job. A bulb is nothing more than resistance placed in the path on purpose, a filament so thin that current struggling through it climbs to thousands of degrees and glows. That is the crude version of the idea: make the circuit fight itself, and take the heat or the light that comes off. The interesting version arrived when circuits stopped merely carrying power and started carrying decisions. In 1947, at Bell Labs, John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley built the transistor: a lump of semiconductor, no moving parts, in which one small current controls a much larger one. That makes a transistor a switch that another circuit can flip. Wire enough of them together and a loop can add, compare, remember, and choose. Success created its own problem, and the engineers of the day named it the tyranny of numbers. Every transistor had to be soldered to its neighbors by hand. A genuinely useful machine wanted thousands of them, and thousands of hand made joints meant thousands of chances to fail. Reliability collapsed exactly as ambition rose. The answer came in 1958. Jack Kilby, newly hired at Texas Instruments, had no vacation days saved and was left almost alone in the lab through the company shutdown, with time to think. Instead of wiring separate components together, he proposed carving the entire circuit, transistors and resistors and connections alike, out of one block of semiconductor. In September he switched his rough prototype on and it worked. Months later, at Fairchild Semiconductor, Robert Noyce reached the same conclusion in silicon and paired it with a flat manufacturing process that could print such circuits by the batch. Between them they had invented the integrated circuit. Kilby received the Nobel Prize for it in 2000. Noyce had died a decade earlier and could not share it. Everything since has been the same trick, performed smaller. The chip in an ordinary phone now carries tens of billions of transistors, each one a switch on a loop, packed into a chip the size of a fingernail. None of it has escaped Volta's rule. It is still a source, still a path, still a return. Break it anywhere and the light goes out.
